bib.title: Inference-Time Amplification of Weak Reasoning Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Inference-Time Amplification of Weak Reasoning Models", Varun Sunkaraneni (first author, equal contribution with Pierfrancesco Beneventano), Riccardo Neumarker, Tomaso Poggio, Tomer Galanti. Texas A&M / MIT. Preprint (arXiv 2605.14163v2, 4 Oct 2026; v1 presumably May 2026, which the arXiv ID implies but the PDF does not state). No venue.
COVERAGE: 30 of 30 pages read; 102,460 chars extracted. I read main text, proofs (A.1.4 closely, others skimmed), implementation details C, results D, tables 1-8. References were skimmed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Selection, not sampling, bounds how much exposed capability is recovered. Oracle-gap recovery = (system - pass@1)/(oracle@k - pass@1).
  number: 78.3% recovered
  setup: SWE-bench Verified, 500 tasks, GPT-5.4 nano Mini-SWE-agent, k=8, critic-gated pairwise comparator, hidden tests never shown to the selector
  quote: "A single headline trajectory resolves 67.0% of tasks. Full critic–comparator orchestration reaches 76.4%, while an oracle that chooses a passing patch whenever one is present reaches 79.0%. The implemented system therefore recovers 78.3% of the improvement exposed by eight proposals."
  where: p.7 (section 7.1)
- Most residual failures are proposal failures, not selection failures.
  number: 89.0% / 11.0%
  setup: as above, k=8
  quote: "Among the tasks the system still misses, 89.0% contain no passing patch in the eight-proposal pool and 11.0% are oracle-reachable selection misses."
  where: p.7
- Giving the judge more evidence raises recovery with the proposals held fixed.
  number: comparator edge 0.04 to 0.09; recovery 24% to 40%; solve rate 67.0% to 69.6%
  setup: Qwen3.6-27B SWE-bench pool, oracle 79.2%; patch-only vs patch plus repository access
  quote: "Repository access raises ˆσ from 0.04 to 0.09, solve rate from 67.0% to 69.6%, and oracle-gap recovery from 24% to 40%."
  where: p.9 (Fig 3c); judgment latency rose from 178 s to 739 s (Fig 4c, read off the figure text)
- A cheap sound verifier beats a learned judge.
  number: 99.0% for both; 6.3x fewer tokens
  setup: Blocksworld, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 598 tasks, 5 proposals; first proposal solves 59.5%
  quote: "a public plan checker reaches the same 99.0% success as the learned committee on the saved five-proposal pool while using substantially fewer model tokens"; also "When a cheap sound verifier exists, it should be preferred to learned judging."
  where: p.27-28 (D.7, Fig 6)
- A misaligned judge can make things worse than doing nothing.
  number: 80.5% to 73.0% (comparators-only 72.7)
  setup: CommonGen, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 992 tasks, exact concept coverage required
  quote: "comparator-based selection is misaligned with exact required-concept coverage and reduces success from 80.5% to 73.0%."
  where: p.28
- Simple heuristics are unstable. Judges beat them on 3 of 4 SWE pools.
  number: shortest patch 62.8% on Gemma vs 29.4% on Qwen-A3B
  setup: SWE-bench, k=8, 4 proposer pools (Table 4)
  quote: "shortest-patch selection reaches 62.8% on Gemma but only 29.4% on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B pool."
  where: p.26. Gemma-4-31B is the exception: heuristic 62.8 vs committee 61.0 (Table 4).
- Recovery varies by proposer pool and domain (comparator-only, r=3, k=8).
  number: SWE 69% nano, 46% Qwen-27B, 58% Qwen-A3B, 27% Gemma; MATH L4-5 85%; GSM-Plus 77%; LiveCodeBench 46%; miniF2F-hard 43%
  quote: "at k = 8, recovery is 69%, 46%, 58%, and 27% for nano, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Gemma-4-31B, respectively."
  where: p.26 (Table 2). On MATH/GSM, Qwen2.5 proposers are judged by Qwen3-1.7B, and the baseline there is majority vote (66.9 on GSM, committee 75.5).
- Pairwise comparison scales with the pool; pointwise scoring saturates.
  number: GSM-Plus pairwise recovery 76.7-79.5% for k=2,4,8; critic top-score tie rate 55.6% to 92.6%
  setup: one saved 8-proposal GSM-Plus pool, subset-averaged; oracle 49.1 to 83.6
  quote: "the pointwise critic increasingly loses resolution: its top-score tie rate rises from 55.6% to 92.6%."
  where: p.26 (Table 3)
- Returns on more judging are flat after a little. Oracle also stalls.
  number: 1 comparator vote/pair 75.48% at $0.969/task; 3 votes 76.16% at $1.104; oracle 79.0% to 79.2% at k=8 to 16
  setup: fixed nano SWE pool
  quote: "One comparator vote per pair reaches 75.48% at $0.97 per task, and three votes reach 76.16% at $1.10; additional judging brings little further improvement." And "Doubling the proposal budget from k = 8 to 16 raises the oracle only from 79.0% to 79.2%".
  where: p.8-9
- Critic gate: a permissive gate helps, a strict one hurts.
  number: no gate 75.8%; drop 0-yes patches 76.4%; unanimous gate 76.0%
  quote: "a permissive critic gate improves on pure Copeland, while stricter gates begin to remove useful patches."
  where: p.25 (Table 1)
  Aggregation rule is secondary: "differ by at most one percentage point." Single-elimination bracket was worse at 74.6%.
- Theory: coverage alone gives no identifiability. A weak comparator edge sigma > 1/2 can be amplified by repetition. Local errors add over the trajectory.
  number: error bound eps_loc <= eps_prop + k^2 e^{-2r sigma^2}; end-to-end err <= L_x * eps
  quote: "Thus the selector need not be highly accurate in a single comparison: a uniformly better-than-chance local preference can be amplified by repetition."
  where: p.5-6 (Thm 2, Cor 2)
- A verifier of finished outputs does not imply a good local critic for intermediate steps (NP-hardness argument).
  quote: "The existence of an efficient verifier for completed outputs is substantially weaker than Assumption 2."
  where: p.17 (Prop 2)
- The paper recommends reporting pass@1, oracle@k, system result and recovery together. It says pass@1 alone conflates proposal quality with selection. (p.30)

LIMITS: Experiments mostly test terminal selection, not multi-step composition. Finite-k oracle failure only upper-bounds the blind-spot floor. Cross-task comparisons are descriptive, since proposers, judges and tasks differ. The miniF2F gain is "suggestive rather than conclusive (p = 0.064)". The IFBench run is incomplete and excluded. Cost comparison with Opus 4.5 is "not a controlled cost comparison". Judge cost is only 2.8% of tokens on SWE but 98% on MATH/GSM, so cheap selection does not generalize. The one-sided critic is an idealization. The headline 76.4% is a separate run from the r=3 comparator-only replay (75.7%). The recovery denominator is small for weak pools, so ratios are noisy.

BUILDS ON: boosting (Schapire 1990; Freund & Schapire 1995/1997); self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023); Large Language Monkeys (Brown et al., 2024); verifiers (Cobbe et al., 2021); process reward models (Lightman et al., 2024); LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023); weak-to-strong (Burns et al., 2024); iterated amplification (Christiano et al., 2018); SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024).

CODE: none in the paper. The protocol is in prose (C.2): "For each unordered pair (pi, pj), we query the comparator in both presentation orders. A pair is counted as a win for pi only if both orders... select pi... Disagreement, a tie, or a missing response is treated as a tie." Copeland score selects the winner, and ties break by proposal index. The comparator prompt asks for a failure hypothesis first. A parse failure counts as abstain or tie. This is on p.23.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p.8): (a) SWE scaling, (b) selectors at k=8 from 67.0 to 79.0 (visible-test filter 71.2, critics only 72.0, comparators only 75.8), (c) GSM-Plus. It shows the selector ladder against the oracle best explained visually.
- Fig 3 (p.8): recovery by configuration, boundary cases, fixed-coverage intervention. Best for the scorekeeper note.
- Fig 4 (p.9): cost against accuracy.
- Fig 6 (p.28): Blocksworld, verifier vs committee token cost.

FIT: Note 03-the-scorekeeper is the right target. The verifier-first rule, judge failure modes, miscalibration and the evidence-richer judge all belong there. Two secondary fits: 09-failure-modes-and-guardrails (misaligned judge reduces performance), and 02-loop-shapes if best-of-k or sampling-then-select is a loop shape there. I did not read those notes.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Text extraction is clean apart from run-together words in the title and equations. Figure data came from extracted figure text, not images. I did not run the figures.py captions script.
